section_summary: This section focuses on U.S. and Japanese discussions concerning the organization, operational effectiveness, and possible centralization of the Japanese police system in late 1949. It contains communications between General Douglas MacArthur and Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida, journalistic reports from Newsweek on police transportation, intelligence shortcomings, and Communist-led unrest such as the Taira incident, and internal State Department memoranda assessing NSC 13/3 implementation amid SCAP's resistance to altering the decentralized police structure. The section concludes with a detailed discussion between State Department officials and Japanese police liaison Masayoshi Morino exploring jurisdictional hurdles, local security challenges, and the broader political and psychological climate in occupied Japan.

subfiles.about: General MacArthur advises Prime Minister Yoshida on Japanese police reform, emphasizing that police power must derive its strength from serving and being answerable to the people.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur expresses confidence that Japanese police reform will maintain public safety and democratic principles as servants answerable to the people.
subfiles.title: Letter from General Douglas MacArthur to Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida regarding Japanese Police Reorganization

subfiles.about: Harry F. Kern sends W. Walton Butterworth correspondence from Newsweek Tokyo bureau chief Compton Pakenham concerning the Japanese police force.
subfiles.summary: Kern thanks Butterworth for a recent letter, plans an upcoming Washington visit, and encloses Pakenham's correspondence on Japanese police.
subfiles.title: Letter from Harry F. Kern to W. Walton Butterworth

subfiles.about: Marshall Green analyzes Compton Pakenham's observations regarding the Japanese police, highlighting issues of mobility, intelligence, and overdecentralization.
subfiles.summary: Green analyzes Pakenham's observations on police mobility, intelligence needs, and coordination weaknesses arising from an overdecentralized Japanese police system.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Marshall Green to W. Walton Butterworth regarding Comments on Mr. Kern's Letter

subfiles.about: Compton Pakenham reports on popular attitudes, rural grievances, Communist infiltration fears, and severe mobility and intelligence deficiencies affecting the Japanese police.
subfiles.summary: Pakenham examines problems facing Japan's decentralized police, citing rural complaints, fears of Communist infiltration, and severe mobility and intelligence deficiencies demonstrated during the Taira incident and railway strikes, while noting growing public backlash against radical repatriates.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Compton Pakenham on Inadequacies of the Japanese Police Establishment

subfiles.about: B. A. F. summarizes Tokyo Despatch 610 regarding SCAP's rejection of Prime Minister Yoshida's proposals for police reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Reports SCAP's rejection of Yoshida's police reorganization request, noting the Japanese Government nevertheless continues drafting revisions for the Diet.
subfiles.title: Memorandum to Niles W. Bond regarding Tokyo's Despatch No. 610 of September 3, 1949

subfiles.about: Richard L. Sneider evaluates Compton Pakenham's report, focusing on Communist infiltration, non-emergency police coordination, intelligence functions, and mobility.
subfiles.summary: Sneider finds Communist infiltration fears exaggerated, but agrees that police immobility, poor coordination, and pre-treaty intelligence training remain critical problems.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Richard L. Sneider to Marshall Green regarding Comments on Mr. Kern's Letter

subfiles.about: Livingston T. Merchant advises Butterworth that SCAP is unlikely to accept major changes to the police establishment without drastic measures.
subfiles.summary: Merchant attaches earlier correspondence to Voorhees, doubting SCAP can be moved on police reform without drastic pressure; Green comments below.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Livingston T. Merchant to W. Walton Butterworth regarding Japanese Police

subfiles.about: George F. Kennan asks whether Far Eastern Affairs officers wish to use two New York Times clippings to press the Army on Japanese police policy.
subfiles.summary: Kennan asks whether NA officers want to use attached New York Times clippings to squeeze answers from the Army.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip from George F. Kennan to Livingston T. Merchant regarding New York Times Clippings

subfiles.about: Lindesay Parrott reports on Under Secretary of the Army Tracy S. Voorhees's visit to Tokyo and MacArthur's statements on Japanese police strength.
subfiles.summary: Voorhees reviews Japan's relief burden in Tokyo, citing MacArthur's assurances that strengthened Japanese police can control internal disorders without reinforcements.
subfiles.title: Burdens of Japan Upon U.S. Weighed

subfiles.about: A news report describes Tochigi Prefecture Governor Kodaira's proposal to petition SCAP to maintain civil affairs supervision due to weak local police forces.
subfiles.summary: Governor Kodaira and local officials consider petitioning SCAP to retain prefectural civil affairs supervision, fearing weak, unarmed police cannot withstand Communists.
subfiles.title: Japanese May Ask U.S. to Extend Rule

subfiles.about: Butterworth forwards a State Department memorandum on the Japanese police establishment to Under Secretary of the Army Voorhees prior to his trip to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth transmits a police memorandum to Voorhees before his Japan trip, urging discussions with MacArthur on implementing NSC 13/3.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. Walton Butterworth to Tracy S. Voorhees

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum detailing the deficiencies of Japan's decentralized police and urging central coordination and mobile forces under NSC 13/3.
subfiles.summary: Green argues that Japanese police strengthening under NSC 13/3 has been improperly limited to small arms, disputing CINCFE/G-2 claims of adequacy by citing the Taira station seizure, railway sabotage, and Diet resolutions demanding national coordination and mobility.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Marshall Green on The Japanese Police Establishment

subfiles.about: Marshall Green records a discussion between Masayoshi Morino and John M. Allison regarding structural weaknesses of the Japanese police and broader public sentiment.
subfiles.summary: Morino candidly critiques excessive police decentralization, urging a higher ratio of national police, cross-jurisdictional investigative authority, and higher population thresholds for municipal forces, while reflecting on Japanese confusion over democratization, cold war tensions, and American occupation policies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on the Japanese Police
